voices.teen: A relaxed teenage boy, about fifteen, speaking casually to a smart speaker in the evening. Natural and a little bored. Clear studio recording.
voices.asst2: A calm, clear, friendly female smart-speaker assistant voice. Warm, steady, polite and efficient. Clear studio recording.

lines: This is a demonstration of system architecture.
Four ecosystems that were never designed to talk to each other: Apple, Amazon, Meta, and Cloudflare's edge network.
One event travels across all of them, in near real time, and lands in exactly the same place, every time.
The project carrying that event is a simple family board. The architecture underneath it is the real subject.
A sentence is spoken to a phone in the kitchen.
Moments later, it is written on a post-it note, on the living room wall.
No app was opened. Nobody typed a thing.
Here is how that happens, and how six very different systems were taught to work together, like clockwork.
Here is the architecture, end to end.
On the left are the voices: Apple's Siri, Amazon's Alexa, and Meta's AI assistant Muse, which reads the family's calendar and mail.
In the middle is Cloudflare's global edge network.
On the right, every screen in the house.
And at the very centre of it all, one small text file.
Two hash signs start a group, and every group gets its own colour of paper.
A dash and a pair of empty brackets is a task. Put an x inside, and it is crossed out.
Any person can read it. Any AI can write it. And the wall needs no AI at all to understand it.
The shortcut sends one secure request across the internet, to a Cloudflare worker.
It carries a single field: the words that were spoken.
A private write key rides in the header, and the worker checks it in constant time, so even the speed of a rejection gives nothing away.
Next, the worker gathers context from the board itself.
Every group. Every task. The voice changes from the last six hours, and any question it asked in the last three minutes.
All of it goes to Workers AI: Meta's Llama three point three, seventy billion parameters, running on Cloudflare's own GPUs.
The model must answer in a strict JSON shape: an action, a group, a task, and a question, if it is not sure.
But the AI never gets the final word.
Tasks are trimmed to thirty-nine characters, so they always fit on a note.
And before anything is crossed off, exactly one matching task must really exist. If not, the board simply asks: which one?
Then, the heart of the system: a Cloudflare Durable Object, called Board.
There is exactly one of it, anywhere in the world, so two people can never overwrite each other.
It adds one line, and leaves every other byte exactly as it was.
It saves the file to its own built-in SQLite database, and remembers the change, so that undo just works.
The same object is holding an open WebSocket to every screen in the house.
It pushes the whole file down every one of them, at the same moment.
No polling. No refresh button. The note simply appears.
On the living room TV, the board reads the file, and finds the Appointments group.
It writes the new line in handwriting, on a three-dimensional sheet of paper, pinned to the wall.
It even understands dates. Today's tasks are highlighted and stamped. Overdue to-dos turn red. Past events quietly fade.
Back in the kitchen, the phone reads the answer aloud.
Added Dentist, Thursday 4 PM, to Appointments. Anything else?
The conversation carries on until you say you're done. And if you say undo, the board remembers exactly what you meant.
Six in the evening. Another family member, and a completely different ecosystem.
What should I update on the family board?
Amazon's cloud turns that speech into an intent, called Done Intent, holding the words: the math packet.
Then it signs the request with its own certificate.
The worker verifies everything. The certificate really comes from Amazon. Its name is echo API dot amazon dot com. The RSA signature matches.
The request is less than a hundred and fifty seconds old. And the skill ID belongs to this family.
Only then does the intent become a sentence, and travel through exactly the same brain that Siri uses.
On every screen, a pen stroke crosses out the math packet.
Crossed off Math packet in School. Anything else?
Two very different ecosystems. One shared memory.
Some tasks are never spoken at all.
Meta's AI assistant Muse reads Apple Calendar, Gmail and Apple Mail: appointments, school notices, deliveries.
It rewrites the whole file by the house rules, and uploads it in a single request.
The worker checks the key, the format, the encoding and the size. The object saves it, and every screen has it, instantly.
Every screen also carries a safety net.
If the live connection ever drops, the board checks every two seconds, and reconnects with a growing wait: one second, two, four, up to a minute.
While connected, it still checks once a minute, just in case.
A keep-alive ping every thirty seconds is answered by Cloudflare itself, without waking the object, so a quiet screen costs nothing.
Every part runs to a clock.
Three minutes to answer a follow-up question. Five minutes between lighting updates.
Three hours before a finished note peels off the wall. Six hours of voice memory.
And at midnight, every note is read again, for what is due today.
It follows the real sun: amber at sunrise and sunset, and a lamp-lit night that dims after ten.
Autumn leaves fall. Snow arrives for Christmas, and hearts for Valentine's week.
Butterflies visit by day, and land on the notes, shadows and all.
And it only redraws when something moves, so the graphics chip can rest.
Look closer, and the same architectural patterns appear again and again.
Event driven. Every change begins as a single event, from any ecosystem.
A single writer. One Durable Object puts every change in order, so the state is always consistent.
Compute at the edge. No servers to manage, and always close to the person speaking.
AI with guardrails. The model interprets, but deterministic code decides.
Push, not poll. State flows to every screen the moment it changes, with polling only as a fallback.
And zero trust between vendors. A shared secret for Apple and Muse, signed certificates for Amazon.
Step back, and this is the whole machine.
Two voice assistants. An AI collector. A serverless edge worker. A seventy billion parameter language model. One strongly consistent object, with its own database. And a live line to every screen.
Every piece is secured. Every piece can be replaced. And all of them turn together.
One event. Four ecosystems. Near real time.
A system architecture demonstration, designed, integrated, and engineered end to end.
